name: Horsetail
habitat: Wet ground — ditches, stream banks, damp railway embankments, sandy wet waste ground.
identify: Jointed, hollow, ridged green stems with whorls of thin needle-like branches at each joint — like a bottle brush or a horse's tail.
The joints pull apart cleanly with an audible pop and slot back together.
Gritty to the touch and it will actually scour a pot — the tissue is loaded with silica, which is where the old name 'scouring rush' comes from.
In spring a separate pale unbranched fertile stem appears with a cone at the tip, before the green ones.

lookalikes.name: Marsh horsetail
lookalikes.danger: Contains the alkaloid palustrine and is toxic to livestock; not one to use.
lookalikes.tell: Marsh horsetail has FEWER, coarser branches and a much larger central hollow relative to stem width; it grows in wetter ground. If you cannot tell them apart, do not use either internally.

preparations.method: Crush the fresh green stems and apply to the wound.
preparations.for_use: A styptic and astringent for shallow bleeding.
A wash for wounds and skin. Also the traditional internal use as a diuretic, which is the use with the most caution attached.

preparations.method: Use dried stems as a scourer or fine sandpaper.
preparations.for_use: Cleaning a pot or smoothing a bow-drill spindle.

cautions: Horsetail contains THIAMINASE, which destroys vitamin B1. Sustained internal use causes thiamine deficiency; it has poisoned livestock this way. Do not drink it regularly.
Also a strong diuretic — a bad idea when you are already short of water.
Some populations concentrate selenium and other minerals from the soil.
Avoid internally in pregnancy, in kidney disease, and with alcohol.
evidence: The silica and astringency are real and the topical styptic use is traditional and widespread. The internal safety concerns are documented and are the reason this entry leans topical.
